en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Food, 38.
The Training Rule on Storing Up.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Ānanda’s preceptor, the Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa, was dwelling in the forest.
Having gone for alms, he would bring dried kura rice to the monastery, dry it, and set it aside.
Whenever he had need of food, he would moisten it again and again with water and eat it; he entered the village for alms only after a long time.
The bhikkhus said to the venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa,
"Friend, why do you enter the village for alms so late?
Then the venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa informed the bhikkhus of the matter.
“But, friend, do you eat food that has been stored up?
“Yes, friend.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How can the venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa eat food that has been stored up? ...
[and so on] ... “Is it true, Belaṭṭhasīsa, that you eat food that has been stored up?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, Belaṭṭhasīsa, eat food that has been stored up?
This, Belaṭṭhasīsa, is neither for the inspiration of those without confidence nor for the increase of those with confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, a monk should eat or consume fresh or cooked food that has been stored, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however...
Whoever is such... [as previously described] ...a bhikkhu...
this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu."
"Storing up" means that what was received today is eaten on the following day.
"Edible food" means:
There are five kinds of food: excluding those that are for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for life, the remainder is called "hard food" (khādanīya).
"Soft food" (bhojanīya) refers to these five foods: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
If one receives [food] thinking, “I will eat it, I will consume it,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food while perceiving that it has been stored for more than a day, there is an offense of expiation.
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food while it is in storage, and one is in doubt [as to whether it is in storage], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food while it is in storage, perceiving it to be not in storage, there is an offense of expiation.
If one accepts for the purpose of food anything that is to be used within a watch of the night, for seven days, or for life, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not stored, but one perceives it as being stored, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not stored, but one is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one stores what is not for storage and perceives it as not for storage.
There is no offense if one stores what is for the duration of the day and eats it within that same time.
If one stores what is to be used within the watch of the night and eats it during that watch;
if one stores what is to be used for seven days and eats it within those seven days;
or if one uses what is to be kept for life when there is a requisite need.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The eighth training rule concerning the storing of food is finished.
